240.text:
Animals are kept on farms, in zoos, in laboratories and in homes, and some people argue that the laws protecting them should be stronger. I largely agree, since animals can feel pain and fear, although laws must also take account of human needs.

To begin with, animals can feel pain and fear, so they deserve legal protection. Weak laws allow cruelty on farms, in circuses and in laboratories, whereas strong laws set minimum standards of care and penalties for those who break them. In some places, for example, hens may be kept in tiny cages for their entire lives, and a law that bans such cages forces producers to give animals room to move. Without legal limits, businesses that want to cut costs may be tempted to ignore suffering, and honest producers are undercut by careless ones.

Furthermore, clear rules reflect the values of a modern society. Most people agree that causing needless suffering is wrong, yet individuals cannot inspect farms or laboratories themselves, so only inspectors acting under strict laws can ensure that standards are kept. Better conditions can also lead to healthier animals and safer food. However, the laws must be realistic. Farmers who face higher costs may need time and financial support to adapt, and some research that depends on animals may save human lives, so such work should be allowed under strict supervision. Strong laws should therefore protect animals without ignoring the needs of people who depend on them.

In conclusion, animal welfare laws should be strengthened to a large extent, because animals can suffer and weak rules allow cruelty, provided that the changes are introduced fairly.

304.text:
Wildlife conservation is often seen as a luxury that benefits animals more than people. I agree that it has improved people's lives, since healthy ecosystems provide practical services and many communities earn a living from protected nature.

To begin with, wildlife conservation improves people's lives in practical ways. Healthy ecosystems pollinate crops, clean water and reduce floods, and these services would cost enormous sums to replace artificially. Bees that pollinate fruit trees, for example, help farmers to harvest more apples and almonds without any extra cost. Forests and wetlands protected for wildlife also store water and reduce the damage caused by storms. In addition, wild plants and animals provide the basis for new medicines, so losing a species may mean losing a future treatment.

Furthermore, conservation creates jobs and income. Nature tourism brings visitors to national parks and reserves, and local people work as guides, rangers, drivers and hotel staff. When communities share in these earnings, they have a reason to protect wildlife instead of hunting or clearing the land. Contact with nature also benefits mental health and offers children a chance to learn about the living world. Admittedly, conservation sometimes restricts land use and can cause conflict, as when elephants damage crops, but compensation schemes and community involvement can reduce these problems. Overall, the benefits to people, in food, water, income and wellbeing, are considerable and far-reaching.

In conclusion, I agree that wildlife conservation has improved people's lives, because it supports essential natural services and provides income, provided that local communities share fairly in the gains.

437.text:
Plastic waste, overfishing and rising temperatures are damaging the world's seas, and some people believe that ocean conservation should be a global priority. I largely agree, since the ocean is shared by all countries and supports human life, although other urgent problems must not be neglected.

To begin with, the ocean is a shared resource that no single country can protect alone. Fish stocks, currents and pollution cross borders, so action by one nation can be undone by another. Fishing fleets that empty a region's waters, for example, leave coastal communities in other countries with fewer fish. Only international agreements, shared monitoring and common rules can prevent such harm. A global priority also encourages richer countries to help poorer ones to protect their coastlines.

Furthermore, the sea provides food for billions of people and helps to regulate the climate and produce oxygen. If marine ecosystems collapse, millions of people who depend on fishing and coastal tourism would lose their income and their main source of protein. Healthy oceans also absorb large amounts of carbon dioxide, which slows climate change. However, ocean conservation cannot be the only priority. Governments also face poverty, health care and education, and enforcement across huge areas of open water is difficult. Realistic goals, such as protected zones, catch limits and stronger rules on plastic, together with funding for poorer countries, would make conservation both effective and fair.

In conclusion, ocean conservation should be a global priority to a large extent, because the sea is shared and essential for human life, provided that it is balanced with other urgent needs.

452.text:
Some countries have strict laws against cruelty to animals while others have almost none, and some argue that stricter animal protection laws benefit society as well as animals. I largely agree, although the benefits depend on laws being enforced fairly.

To begin with, stricter animal protection laws benefit society as well as animals. Respect for animals teaches children compassion, and researchers have found links between cruelty to animals and violence towards people, so laws that take cruelty seriously may help to prevent wider harm. Better conditions on farms can also reduce the risk of disease spreading among animals and into the human population, and they improve food safety. A farm that keeps animals in clean, spacious housing, for example, usually needs fewer antibiotics, which helps to slow the spread of drug-resistant infections.

Furthermore, strong laws support the economy in certain areas. Countries with good records on animal welfare attract responsible tourists and consumers who are willing to pay more for ethical products, and businesses that meet high standards gain a reputation for quality. Clear rules also create a level playing field, so that careful producers are not undercut by careless ones. However, stricter laws can raise costs for farmers and small businesses, and enforcement requires trained inspectors, which governments must fund. Support, advice and transition periods can reduce the burden on producers. If these conditions are met, the gains for society, in health, values and trade, clearly outweigh the costs.

In conclusion, stricter animal protection laws benefit society to a large extent, since they promote compassion, safer food and fair competition, provided that they are enforced fairly and supported by help for producers.

122.text:
Cities offer jobs and services, but many of them lack parks, trees and open space, which makes life hotter, noisier and less healthy. This essay will suggest practical measures that governments could take, focusing on protecting and creating green space and on keeping it well maintained and accessible.

To begin with, governments can protect and expand green space inside cities. Planning rules can protect existing parks, require new developments to include gardens and playgrounds, and encourage green roofs and street trees where land is scarce. Unused sites, such as old car parks or empty plots, can be turned into small parks at low cost. A block of flats with a planted roof, for example, stays cooler in summer and offers residents a small garden. Over time, a network of connected green areas can help to cool the city, absorb pollution and shelter birds and insects.

In addition, authorities should make sure that green spaces are well maintained and accessible to everyone. Parks that are dirty or unsafe are rarely used, so councils need to budget for cleaning, lighting, repair and sensible security. Facilities such as paths, benches and play areas should be suitable for children, older people and people with disabilities, and parks should be located in poorer districts as well as wealthy ones. Equally important, involving residents in the design and care of their local park, through volunteer groups or consultations, encourages pride and reduces vandalism. These measures are inexpensive compared with the health and social benefits that they bring.

In conclusion, protecting and creating green spaces and then maintaining them for all residents offers the most realistic way of improving urban green areas.

207.text:
As cities grow, public gardens are sometimes sold for housing or shops, and many people say that they should be protected from development. I agree with this view, since gardens give city residents health, shade and a place to meet that cannot easily be replaced.

To begin with, public gardens give city residents health, shade and a place to meet. They cool the air in summer, absorb dust and pollution, shelter birds and insects and offer free space to rest, exercise and play. For people who live in flats without a garden, these places are often the only contact with nature. A small garden in a crowded district, for example, may be used every day by older residents, parents with young children and office workers on their lunch break. Studies of many cities suggest that access to green space improves physical and mental health.

Furthermore, once a garden has been built over, it is almost impossible to replace. New trees need decades to mature, and the history and community life of the site are lost for good. Housing, by contrast, can usually be built on empty or abandoned sites, or on land that has already been developed, so protecting gardens does not mean stopping growth. Admittedly, cities need more homes and economic activity, and some gardens may be poorly used or badly kept. In such cases, authorities should improve them instead of selling them, and any development that does take place should be limited and balanced by new green space elsewhere.

In conclusion, I agree that public gardens should be protected from development, because they are valuable and irreplaceable, although well-planned building on other sites should continue.

276.text:
In many cities, small plots of land are used by residents to grow vegetables, herbs and flowers together. This essay will outline two key ways in which community gardens benefit neighbourhoods: by bringing people together and by providing fresh food and green space.

First and foremost, community gardens bring neighbours together. Residents grow vegetables on unused land, share skills and tools, and meet people from different backgrounds, which strengthens friendships and reduces loneliness. A vacant plot turned into a vegetable garden, for example, can become a place where neighbours meet instead of a spot where rubbish collects. Children learn where food comes from, and older residents pass on knowledge and enjoy the company. Working on a shared project builds trust, so neighbourhoods with such gardens often feel safer and friendlier, and people are more willing to help one another.

In addition, community gardens provide fresh food and improve the local environment. Households that grow their own produce save money on groceries and eat more vegetables, which supports healthy diets, especially in areas with few fresh food shops. The gardens also turn neglected land into green space that cools the air, shelters insects and birds and absorbs rainwater. Gardening is a gentle form of exercise and can reduce stress, which benefits mental wellbeing. Although a garden needs volunteers and some funding for tools and water, councils can help by lending land and offering advice, and the benefits to the neighbourhood far outweigh the small cost.

To sum up, community gardens benefit neighbourhoods by building community spirit and by providing fresh food and green space. For these reasons, they deserve continued public support.

429.text:
Beaches are among the most popular public places, but many coastlines are now being lined with hotels, apartments and private clubs. I agree that public beaches should be preserved from development, since they are a shared resource that protects the coast and should stay open to everyone.

To begin with, public beaches should stay open to everyone. Building along the shore privatises access, so that ordinary families are shut out of places that were once free to enjoy. Beaches offer cheap recreation and exercise for people of all incomes, and restricting access creates a divide between those who can afford a sea view and those who cannot. A resort that blocks the path to the water with fences and security guards, for example, turns a public place into a private one. Once access is lost, it is rarely regained.

Furthermore, building on or near the shore damages the natural features that protect people and wildlife. Sand dunes act as barriers against storms and floods, and construction can remove them, speed up erosion and increase the risk to nearby homes. Lights, noise and crowds also disturb nesting birds and turtles. Well-managed beaches keep attracting visitors and income without permanent damage. Admittedly, development brings jobs and tourist spending, and some facilities such as toilets and cafes are useful. However, a limited amount of simple, low-impact building set back from the shore can provide most of these benefits, while keeping the beach itself open and natural.

In conclusion, I agree that public beaches should be preserved from development, because they belong to everyone and protect the coast, although small, carefully planned facilities can be allowed.
